subject: Environment
topic: Green technology and renewable energy II — mixed tiers
description: Solar, wind, green hydrogen, carbon capture, India's RE targets

questions.stem: India's National Solar Mission was launched as part of which broader climate-action plan?

options.option_text: Green India Mission
National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC)
Swachh Bharat Mission
Jal Jeevan Mission

questions.explanation: NAPCC (launched 2008) is India's flagship climate-policy umbrella with EIGHT National Missions — Solar (JNNSM), Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change. JNNSM's revised target (2015) — 100 GW solar by 2022 (not fully met); overall renewable 500 GW by 2030 is the current headline. Green India Mission is a SEPARATE mission within NAPCC.

questions.stem: 'Green hydrogen' differs from 'grey hydrogen' primarily in that it is produced by:

options.option_text: Steam methane reforming of natural gas
Electrolysis of water using renewable electricity
Coal gasification
Direct synthesis from air

questions.explanation: Hydrogen-colour palette — 'green' H₂ is produced by electrolysis of water powered by renewables (zero CO₂); 'grey' H₂ from steam-methane reforming (most today); 'blue' H₂ is grey + carbon capture; 'brown/black' H₂ is from coal gasification. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (Jan 2023) targets 5 million tonnes of green H₂ production annually by 2030.

questions.stem: India's first and largest solar park is located in:

options.option_text: Jodhpur, Rajasthan
Bhadla, Rajasthan
Pavagada, Karnataka
Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh

questions.explanation: Bhadla Solar Park in Jodhpur district, Rajasthan — capacity ~2,245 MW — was completed in 2020 and is one of the largest solar installations in the world. Rajasthan's high solar irradiance and flat terrain suit it well. Pavagada (Karnataka, ~2,050 MW) and Kurnool (AP, ~1,000 MW) are close runners. India's total installed solar capacity has crossed 80 GW (2024).

questions.stem: Which Indian state leads in installed wind-power capacity?

options.option_text: Rajasthan
Tamil Nadu
Gujarat
Maharashtra

questions.explanation: Tamil Nadu has historically led — the Muppandal Wind Farm in Kanyakumari is one of the country's largest. Gujarat has overtaken TN in recent years for new capacity additions (Bhavnagar, Kachchh). Top wind states (2024) — Gujarat and Tamil Nadu are near-equal; Karnataka, Maharashtra, Rajasthan follow. India's total wind capacity is ~45 GW. Offshore wind projects off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu coasts are being developed.

questions.stem: The International Solar Alliance (ISA), co-founded by India in 2015, has its headquarters in:

options.option_text: Paris
Gurugram (India)
Geneva
Abu Dhabi

questions.explanation: ISA — launched at the 2015 Paris Climate Summit by PM Modi and French President Hollande — has its HQ at the National Institute of Solar Energy campus in Gurugram, Haryana. It is the first inter-governmental organisation HQ in India. Originally open to 121 sunshine-rich countries between the Tropics; now membership is open to all UN members (124+ signatories).

questions.stem: Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) technology works by:

options.option_text: Absorbing CO₂ from trees and burying it
Capturing CO₂ from industrial sources and storing it underground
Converting CO₂ directly to oxygen in the atmosphere
Using bacteria to break CO₂ into elements

questions.explanation: CCS traps CO₂ at industrial sources (power plants, cement, steel), compresses it, and injects it into deep geological formations — depleted oil/gas reservoirs, saline aquifers, basalt rock. CCU (Capture and Utilisation) uses it in products like carbonated drinks, concrete. Direct Air Capture (DAC) pulls CO₂ from ambient air — newer, much costlier per tonne. IPCC considers CCS essential for hard-to-abate sectors (steel, cement, heavy industry).

questions.stem: 'Net zero' emissions, a common target in climate policy, means:

options.option_text: No emissions at all
Emissions are balanced by equivalent removals
Emissions fall by half
Emissions are traded internationally

questions.explanation: Net-zero — residual emissions from hard-to-abate activities are matched by CO₂ removals (afforestation, CCS, direct air capture) so the NET balance is zero. Not literally zero emissions. India's target — net zero by 2070 (announced Nov 2021 at COP-26). Global goal to meet Paris 1.5 °C — net zero by ~2050 for major economies. Corporate 'net-zero' pledges often rely heavily on carbon offsets, which are contested.

questions.stem: PM-KUSUM (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan) scheme is primarily designed to benefit which sector by providing solar energy support?

options.option_text: Urban residents seeking rooftop solar installation subsidies
Farmers for solarising irrigation pumps and grid feeders
Industrial units requiring captive green power certificates
Railways for electrification of rural branch line zones

questions.explanation: PM-KUSUM has three components: solarising standalone irrigation pumps, solarising grid-connected pumps, and adding solar capacity on barren land by farmers — all targeted at the agricultural sector. Urban rooftop subsidies fall under PM Surya Ghar, not PM-KUSUM.

questions.stem: The 'PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana', launched by the Government of India in February 2024, aims to supply free electricity up to how many units per month to eligible households through rooftop solar?

options.option_text: Up to 100 units per month free to urban BPL card holders
Up to 200 units per month free to rural households only
Up to 300 units per month free to one crore households
Up to 500 units per month free to industrial cooperatives

questions.explanation: PM Surya Ghar targets one crore households and promises up to 300 units of free electricity per month through rooftop solar installations with central subsidy support. The 200-unit figure is a common distractor arising from earlier pilot scheme proposals.

questions.stem: Green ammonia is attracting attention as a zero-carbon shipping fuel and fertiliser feedstock. Which element, sourced from air, is combined with green hydrogen to synthesise it?

options.option_text: Oxygen separated cryogenically from atmospheric air streams
Carbon dioxide captured from industrial stack emissions
Methane reformed catalytically under high-pressure conditions
Nitrogen extracted from air via an air separation unit

questions.explanation: Ammonia is NH₃ — three hydrogen atoms bonded to one nitrogen atom. Green ammonia uses green hydrogen (electrolysis-based) plus nitrogen separated from air, then combines them via the Haber-Bosch process. CO₂ is used for green methanol, not ammonia; methane reforming produces grey or blue hydrogen, not green ammonia.

questions.stem: India submitted an updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to the UNFCCC in 2022. What is the revised target for non-fossil-fuel share of cumulative installed electric power capacity by 2030?

options.option_text: 40% non-fossil installed capacity, as per the original 2015 NDC
50% cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources
60% of total electricity generation from renewable sources by 2030
45% reduction in emissions intensity compared to 2005 GDP levels

questions.explanation: India's 2022 updated NDC raised the non-fossil capacity target from 40% (2015 NDC) to 50% by 2030. Option D (45% emissions-intensity reduction) is also part of the same updated NDC but pertains to intensity, not installed capacity share — a common mix-up. The 60% generation figure is not an NDC target.

questions.stem: Pumped-storage hydropower is often called the 'grid battery of the world' because it stores electrical energy through which operating mechanism?

options.option_text: Compressing air into underground caverns using off-peak surplus power
Pumping water to an upper reservoir when surplus, releasing it to regenerate power
Charging lithium-ion battery banks during periods of excess generation
Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen via overnight electrolysis

questions.explanation: Pumped-storage plants use surplus electricity (often from solar or wind) to pump water from a lower to an upper reservoir, storing energy as gravitational potential. When demand rises, water is released through turbines to regenerate electricity. Compressed-air energy storage (CAES) is a separate technology; lithium-ion and hydrogen storage are different systems entirely.

questions.stem: The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which is set to affect Indian exports of steel, aluminium and fertilisers, works by imposing which specific type of charge on imports?

options.option_text: A flat tariff based on the exporting country's stated carbon tax rate
A voluntary fund contributed by importers to offset their supply-chain emissions
A levy matching the EU ETS carbon price on emissions embedded in those imports
A reciprocal charge linked to the bilateral clean-energy trade balance

questions.explanation: CBAM requires importers of covered products to purchase CBAM certificates priced at the prevailing EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) allowance price, adjusted for any carbon price already paid in the country of production. It is neither a flat tariff (it tracks ETS prices) nor voluntary, and is not linked to bilateral trade balances. Indian exporters must declare embedded carbon content precisely.

questions.stem: Grid operators managing high solar-penetration systems worry about the 'duck curve' phenomenon. Which specific operational challenge does the duck curve represent?

options.option_text: Excess overnight wind power causing grid-frequency deviations above 50 Hz
Transmission congestion arising from clustered solar parks in arid regions
Voltage instability in rural feeders caused by rooftop solar reverse power flow
A steep evening demand ramp when solar output collapses but peak load persists

questions.explanation: The 'duck curve' — named after its duck-like shape — shows midday surplus from solar depressing net load, followed by a sharp ramp (the duck's neck) after sunset when solar disappears but evening demand peaks. Grid operators must rapidly bring on flexible, dispatchable generation within minutes. Option A describes a wind-specific frequency issue; Options B and C relate to distribution-level problems, not the system-wide ramping challenge the duck curve describes.
